subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage: Hemant looked at the window. His friends were already playing in the park below. He scribbled the last answers of his maths homework as fast as he could, slammed the notebook shut and ran out. The next day Devika Ma'am returned the books. Two sums had red crosses. "Look at question three, Hemant," she said quietly. He had written 48 where the book said 84, and in the other sum he had left out a zero. He stared at the page. A minute of checking would have caught both, and now he had lost the marks.

qa.q: Which sums did Devika Ma'am mark wrong?
qa.a: She marked two sums wrong, with red crosses.

qa.q: What might Hemant have been feeling when he saw the two red crosses?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and annoyed with himself. He stared at the page because he knew he could have caught the errors.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Hemant use to check his work quickly, and why?
qa.a: He could read each answer once against the book before closing the notebook. A short check is enough to catch copying slips.

qa.q: How does Devika Ma'am see the two wrong sums?
qa.a: Devika Ma'am sees careless copying errors, not a gap in understanding. That is why she pointed calmly at question three.

grounding: A boy scribbles answers to go out and play and skips checking, so the next day the teacher marks two sums wrong for copying errors.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage:
"Chetan! Cricket! We need a bowler!"
"Two minutes, Darshan!" Chetan scribbled the last sums, closed the notebook with a slap, and ran.
"Did you check them?"
"No time. They're right, I'm sure."
Next morning Mrs Pillai handed back the notebooks.
"Chetan, come here." She tapped the page. "The question says 48. You wrote 84. And here, 306 became 360. Both would be right if you'd copied the numbers properly."
"But I knew how to do them!"
"I know you did. One minute of checking would have caught both."
Chetan stared at the two red marks. At break Darshan asked, "Cricket after school?" Chetan said, "After I check."

qa.q: What number did Chetan write instead of 48?
What was Chetan feeling when he stared at the two red marks?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and disappointed, since he knew how to do the sums and lost marks only for copying errors.

qa.q: What small step would have saved Chetan's marks?
qa.a: One minute of checking each number against the question before closing the notebook, even with Darshan waiting.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Chetan's 'After I check'?
qa.a: Darshan may be a little impatient to play, but gets a friend who comes out without worrying about more red marks.

grounding: Shows a boy rushing his sums to go and play, skipping the check, and losing two sums to copying errors a minute would have caught.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish and skipping the checking [Pitfall]
passage: I remember the day I learned to check. It was a Tuesday, and the boys from my building were already shouting from the ground below. 'Yusuf, come on!' I had ten sums left. Ammi said, 'Beta, slowly,' but I raced through them, barely looking at the textbook, shut the notebook and ran. Next day Alka Ma'am called me to her desk. Two sums had big red circles. In one I had written 17 where the book said 71. In the other I had copied a plus as a minus. My method was right both times. 'One minute, Yusuf,' she said. 'That's all checking takes.' I was so embarrassed I didn't go down to play that evening.

qa.q: What did Yusuf write instead of 71?
How did Yusuf feel when he saw the red circles?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, enough to skip playing that evening, because his method was right and only copying slips cost him.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do next time the boys are shouting for him?
qa.a: Take one minute to check each answer against the book before running down, just as Alka Ma'am said.

qa.q: How does Alka Ma'am see Yusuf's mistakes?
qa.a: She sees that his method was right and the errors came from rushing, so she points out that checking takes only a minute.

grounding: Illustrates a boy rushing homework to go and play and losing two sums to copying errors that a minute of checking would have caught.
